metadata.title: From asking to observing. Behavioural measures of socio-emotional and motivational skills in large-scale assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA’s two-stage stratified representative sampling of 15-year-old students and applies sampling and replication weights “in line with recommended PISA procedures” (OECD 2014). The analytic samples are restricted to the PSEC indicators’ required data availability (e.g., non-missing responses for at least 3 items within scales for inconsistency/non-differentiation; and for test-based indicators, students with sufficient test coverage such as restricting performance decline to the first three clusters). For cross-country comparisons and regression models, the authors standardize behavioural indicators using the pooled student population (mean 0, SD 1) and include country fixed effects, which aligns with PISA’s complex design. The manuscript does not report specific weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight method details, so the exact implementation cannot be audited from the text, but the use of PISA weights is explicitly stated.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe a single, unified missing-data handling strategy for the full set of analyses (e.g., whether missingness is handled via listwise deletion across all variables, multiple imputation, or other methods). Instead, it specifies indicator-specific inclusion rules (e.g., inconsistency/non-differentiation computed only for respondents with non-missing responses for at least 3 items in a scale; item non-response uses applicable items; performance-decline uses only the first three clusters to avoid end-of-test non-response). Because the dependent variables are behavioural indicators and achievement outcomes are analysed via regression with explicit non-missing requirements for PSEC indicators and controls, the missing-data approach is partially implicit and not fully documented for all models, representing a reporting gap.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Most analyses are based on PISA 2012, using the core 2-hour paper-based assessment plus a 30-minute background questionnaire. The study derives self-reported PSEC measures from the core questionnaire (perseverance index from five items; effort thermometer from the effort question and a difference-from-hypothetical-effort index). Questionnaire-based behavioural indicators are constructed from core questionnaire items with indicator-specific restrictions: item non-response is computed using applicable items (dropping items conditional on prior items); inconsistency and non-differentiation are computed only for respondents with non-missing responses for at least 3 items within each scale/item set, and inconsistency uses item-rest correlations after reverse-coding. Test-based behavioural indicators include performance decline, estimated from paper-based test responses using only the first three clusters (to reduce bias from end-of-test non-response) and using a random-coefficient model with question and booklet fixed effects; response-time effort is computed from PISA 2012 computer-based assessment log files for countries administering the optional computer-based module, using thresholds (reported mainly for 5s). For longitudinal predictive validity, the subset of countries with follow-up data is restricted to Denmark (PISA 2000–PIAAC), Switzerland (PISA 2000–TREE follow-up), Australia (PISA 2003–LSAY), and Canada (PISA 2000–YITS), with outcome measures at about age 25.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) — paper-based assessment: reading, mathematics, science, and collaborative problem solving
main_findings.target_variable: Contemporaneous academic achievement (reading/math/science/problem solving) associated with PSEC indicators
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 (Model B): self-reported lack of perseverance b≈−0.11 to −0.14 (***), adjusted R-squared ≈0.19–0.31; item non-response b≈−0.27 to −0.34 (***), adjusted R-squared ≈0.21–0.33; performance decline b≈−0.12 to −0.15 (***), adjusted R-squared ≈0.30–0.31; response time effort (5 s) b≈−0.12 to −0.15 (***), adjusted R-squared ≈0.19–0.21. Notes report that a 1 SD change in self-reported lack of perseverance corresponds to ~14%–17% of a SD in achievement, and a 1 SD change in non-response corresponds to ~33%–37% of a SD in achievement.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 the study leveraged self-reported lack of perseverance, non-response, performance decline, and response time effort (5 s) to predict contemporaneous academic achievement across reading, mathematics, science, and collaborative problem solving, finding that all PSEC indicators are negatively associated with achievement and that questionnaire-based non-response shows the strongest association. This indicates that behavioural indicators of socio-emotional and motivational skills—especially effort/engagement proxies like non-response—contain meaningful information for interpreting and monitoring achievement differences, even after controlling for key background characteristics.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) — country-level stability across waves (PISA 2003 vs PISA 2012) for PSEC indicators
main_findings.target_variable: Country-level stability of PSEC indicators over time
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 2: absolute correlations between country averages (PISA 2003 vs 2012) are high for most indicators: self-reported lack of effort in test r=0.842; difference in effort r=0.86; non-differentiation r=0.845; inconsistency r=0.897; instrumental motivation benchmark r=0.945; sense of belonging r=0.714. Lower stability is reported for non-response (absolute correlation r=0.282) and performance decline (absolute correlation r=0.405), with rank correlations also reported (e.g., non-response rank correlation 0.525; performance decline rank correlation 0.526).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003 and PISA 2012 the study leveraged non-response, performance decline, non-differentiation, and inconsistency to assess country-level stability of PSEC indicators over time, finding that most behavioural and self-reported measures show high absolute and rank correlations across waves, while non-response and performance decline are less stable. This indicates that behavioural measures can support longitudinal benchmarking in international monitoring systems, but some indicators may require careful interpretation due to greater sensitivity or measurement variability.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000/2003 longitudinal links to young adulthood outcomes (Denmark: PISA 2000–PIAAC; Switzerland: PISA 2000–TREE; Australia: PISA 2003–LSAY; Canada: PISA 2000–YITS)
main_findings.target_variable: Young-adulthood educational attainment (upper secondary completion and university completion by ~age 25)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 4: performance decline is associated with university completion in Australia (b=−0.070*, adj R²=0.205) and Switzerland (b=−0.074***, adj R²=0.125) and Canada (b=−0.132***, adj R²=0.20), while Denmark shows a non-significant coefficient for university (b=−0.066, adj R²=0.148). For upper secondary completion, performance decline is significant in Australia (b=−0.0093**, adj R²=0.0496) and Denmark (b=−0.045*, adj R²=0.0814). Table 5 (incremental predictive power net of self-reported PSEC): performance decline remains predictive for university in Switzerland (b=−0.071***, adj R²=0.133) and Australia (b=−0.072*, adj R²=0.206) and for upper secondary in Denmark (b=−0.043*, adj R²=0.0823) and Switzerland (b=−0.046, adj R²=0.0627).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using linked PISA longitudinal data for Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, and Canada, the study leveraged performance decline, inconsistency, non-response, and non-differentiation to predict educational attainment by about age 25, finding that performance decline shows the most consistent predictive validity—especially for university completion—and retains significance even after accounting for self-reported perseverance/effort where available. This indicates that behavioural engagement measures derived from test-taking can add incremental information for forecasting long-term educational outcomes, supporting their use in monitoring systems beyond contemporaneous achievement.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether behavioural measures of socio-emotional and motivational skills (PSEC)—constructed from PISA questionnaires and students’ behaviour during the assessment—can complement self-reports in international benchmarking. Using PISA 2012 (with robustness to administration conditions) and country-level comparisons between PISA 2003 and 2012, the authors find weak individual-level correlations across methods but generally high country-level stability for most indicators (e.g., absolute correlations often >0.7), with lower stability for non-response and performance decline. In regressions linking PSEC indicators to contemporaneous achievement, all indicators are negatively associated with reading, mathematics, science, and collaborative problem solving; questionnaire-based non-response shows the strongest association (about 33%–37% of a SD in achievement per 1 SD change). In longitudinal links for Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, and Canada, performance decline is the most consistent predictor of university completion by ~age 25 and shows incremental predictive power net of self-reported measures. Limitations include the absence of a unified missing-data strategy description and the fact that the evidence is correlational/associational rather than causal.
